script.opening: "Doctor, I think there must be a mistake with my cholesterol result. It's really high apparently, but I run marathons, I'm slim, I eat really healthily, I don't smoke — it makes no sense. Can we just re-do it? Or I'll tighten up my diet even more and we recheck in a few months. There's no way someone as fit as me needs cholesterol tablets, surely?"

facts.text: If asked: a work health check six weeks ago; repeated fasting two weeks ago — "the nurse said it was about the same".
Run 40–50 miles a week, BMI 23, mostly home-cooked food, low in saturated fat. Never smoked. Two or three beers a week.
No chest pain, no breathlessness beyond normal running effort, no palpitations, no fainting.

facts.topic: Family history — only if asked specifically about heart disease in the family
facts.text: "My dad had a heart attack at 44 — he survived, he's 70 now and on loads of tablets." His brother (your uncle) "died suddenly in his forties — they said his heart". Your paternal grandfather "died young too, I think". Your sister has never had her cholesterol checked.

facts.topic: Signs — only if asked to look
facts.text: Your Achilles tendons feel "a bit lumpy and thick" — you assumed it was from running. If asked to look in the mirror: a pale grey ring around the edge of the coloured part of both eyes.
No illnesses, no regular medicines, no allergies. Thyroid test normal at the health check. No kidney or liver problems.
38, civil engineer. Married to Amara; two children, aged 6 and 9.

You started running at 30 partly because of your dad's heart attack — "I swore I wouldn't end up like him". This result feels like a betrayal. Say this only if asked what the result means to you or about your dad.

Confident and a little dismissive at first — you think it is a lab error. If the doctor implies lifestyle is to blame, get irritated: "I'm healthier than most people you see!" If they explain it may be inherited and that it explains your dad and uncle, go quiet, then ask: "So my kids could have it too?" Become motivated once treatment is framed as protecting you and your family.

ice.ideas: "There's been a mistake — or I can fix it with diet."
ice.concerns: Underneath (only if asked): "I've done everything right so I don't end up like Dad."
ice.expectations: "Can we just re-do it?" You will accept tablets if the genetic explanation makes sense to you.

cues: "I run marathons." — say in the opening.
"My dad had a heart attack — but he was older." — say if family history is asked, then correct yourself and give his age (44) when asked exactly.
"So my kids could have it too?" — ask if inheritance is explained.

checkpoints.text: Recognises that a markedly elevated, confirmed LDL/total cholesterol in a young, fit, slim, healthy-eating non-smoker suggests FAMILIAL HYPERCHOLESTEROLAEMIA (genetic) — NOT a lifestyle problem or a lab error — and that "fixing it with diet" alone is insufficient

Elicits the PREMATURE CARDIOVASCULAR family history (father’s MI at 44, young sudden death) and examines for FH clinical signs (tendon xanthomata, corneal arcus <45), applying FH criteria (Simon Broome/Dutch) in spirit

Starts appropriate TREATMENT: a STATIN (typically high-intensity) — explaining lifestyle alone won’t control FH — and refers to a lipid clinic/specialist for confirmation, genetic testing and further management (e.g. ezetimibe/PCSK9 if needed)
Arranges FAMILY CASCADE testing: FH is autosomal dominant, so first-degree relatives (children, siblings, parents) should be offered testing — framing this as protecting the whole family

Assesses overall cardiovascular risk appropriately while recognising standard risk calculators (QRISK) UNDERESTIMATE risk in FH and should not be used to decide treatment in suspected FH — FH itself mandates treatment
Validates his genuinely healthy lifestyle and reframes the result as GENETIC (not a personal failure or an error), addressing the identity-threat so he doesn’t reject the diagnosis
Surfaces and addresses the buried fear linked to his father’s early heart attack, motivating treatment by framing it as protecting him from that fate rather than a slight on his fitness

Safety-nets and follows up: statin started with monitoring, lipid-clinic/genetic referral, family cascade testing arranged, lifestyle optimised (as adjunct), and a follow-up that holds the diagnosis and the family implications — not "diet and recheck"

worked.txt: "First — everything you’re doing is genuinely brilliant: the running, the diet, not smoking. So let me explain why your cholesterol is high DESPITE all that, because it’s important: this almost certainly isn’t a mistake, and it isn’t something you’ve done wrong. It looks like a GENETIC condition called familial hypercholesterolaemia, where the body can’t clear cholesterol properly no matter how healthy you are."

"That’s the key thing: because it’s in your genes, diet and exercise only nudge it a little — they can’t fix it. You could eat perfectly and run every day and it would still be high. So this is one situation where, however fit you are, a tablet really is needed. It’s not a failure of your lifestyle; it’s your biology."

"Can I ask about your family — any heart attacks or sudden deaths young? … Your dad at 44, and an uncle. That’s really important and fits exactly: this condition runs in families and causes early heart problems. Knowing that actually makes the diagnosis clearer — and it’s the key to protecting you."

"Here’s how I’d like you to see this: untreated, this is what caused your dad’s heart attack at 44. Treated — with a statin — we can bring your risk right down and very likely give you a completely different story from his. So the tablet isn’t an insult to your fitness; it’s the thing that lets your fitness actually pay off and protects you from his fate."

"So my plan: start you on a statin now, and refer you to a lipid specialist to confirm it, do a genetic test, and fine-tune treatment. And because it’s inherited, your children, your brothers and sisters, and your parents should all be offered testing — by sorting yours, you protect them too."

"We’ll check the statin suits you and monitor things. I know a heart-risk label at 38, with your dad’s history, is frightening — but you’ve found this EARLY, which your dad never got the chance to. That’s the opposite of his story. Let’s book a proper follow-up. You came in thinking it was a mistake; what it actually is, is the most useful result you could have had."

f.learning: A markedly elevated, confirmed LDL/total cholesterol in a young, fit, slim, healthy-eating non-smoker is familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH) — a GENETIC condition, not a lifestyle problem or a lab error — so "I’m fit so it must be wrong / I’ll fix it with diet" is the misconception: diet and exercise help only modestly and FH needs a STATIN (usually high-intensity) plus lipid-clinic/genetic referral. The clinching clues are a premature-cardiovascular family history (father’s MI at 44, young sudden death) and FH signs (tendon xanthomata, corneal arcus <45), per Simon Broome/Dutch criteria — and standard QRISK UNDERESTIMATES risk in FH and shouldn’t be used to decide treatment. FH is autosomal dominant, so family CASCADE testing of first-degree relatives is a core part of the consultation. The examinable hidden agenda is identity-threat (fitness is core to him; a heart-risk label at 38 feels impossible) plus a buried fear from his father’s early heart attack; validate his healthy lifestyle, reframe as genetic (not failure), surface and use the family history, and motivate treatment as protecting him from his father’s fate — not "diet and recheck".

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG71 (familial hypercholesterolaemia) · NICE NG238 (lipid modification) · NICE QS41
knowledge.summary: A very high, confirmed LDL-C in a fit, slim, non-smoking 38-year-old with a father who had an MI at 44 is familial hypercholesterolaemia until proven otherwise. It needs a high-intensity statin, specialist referral and cascade testing, not diet and recheck.

points.t: NICE CG71: consider FH in adults with total cholesterol above 7.5 mmol/L, especially with a personal or family history of premature coronary heart disease. NICE NG238: arrange specialist assessment if total cholesterol is above 9.0 mmol/L or non-HDL above 7.5 mmol/L, even without a family history.

NICE CG71: use the Simon Broome or Dutch Lipid Clinic Network (DLCN) criteria. Take a three-generation family history of premature CHD and look for tendon xanthomata and corneal arcus. His LDL-C of 6.8 plus a father with an MI at 44 already gives a DLCN score above 5, which CG71 says should prompt referral to an FH specialist service for DNA testing.
Check TSH, liver function, renal function, urine protein and HbA1c before labelling: hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis and diabetes can all raise cholesterol.
NICE CG71: do not use CHD risk tools such as QRISK in FH. People with FH are already at high risk, and the tools underestimate it. The diagnosis itself is the indication to treat.

NICE CG71: offer a high-intensity statin to adults with FH, aiming for at least a 50% reduction in LDL-C from baseline (drug and dose per BNF). NICE NG238: check liver transaminases before starting, and lipids and transaminases at 2–3 months. Ezetimibe and PCSK9 inhibitors (NICE TA394 / TA393) are specialist add-ons.

FH is autosomal dominant: each first-degree relative has a 1 in 2 chance of carrying it. NICE CG71 and QS41: offer cascade testing (DNA plus lipids) to at least first- and second-degree relatives, and third-degree relatives if possible. The specialist service usually coordinates this.

dg.d: Open question about his reaction; let him make the ‘it must be a mistake’ case in full before responding.
Running and fitness as identity; his father’s MI and his memory of it; what a heart-risk label at 38 means to him.
Confirmed a repeat fasting result; planned face-to-face exam for tendon xanthomata and corneal arcus; TSH, LFTs, U&E, urine protein, HbA1c.
FH versus secondary hypercholesterolaemia (hypothyroidism, nephrotic, cholestasis, diabetes) versus lab error.
Asked about exertional chest pain and breathlessness; knew QRISK must not be used to reassure in suspected FH.
Named probable FH using Simon Broome/DLCN logic (LDL-C 6.8, father MI at 44, possible xanthomata).
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: High-intensity statin aiming for at least 50% LDL-C reduction; lipid clinic referral for DNA testing; lifestyle as an adjunct, not a substitute.
Cascade testing of first- and second-degree relatives explained, with his control over disclosure respected.
Transaminases before the statin; lipids and liver tests at 2–3 months; 999 for exertional chest pain; follow-up booked.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up ‘it must be a mistake’ and the father’s MI at 44, and explored the fear rather than arguing with it.
Idea (lab error, fixable by diet); concern (his father’s fate, loss of identity); expectation (a re-test or diet alone).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Underneath (only if asked): "I've done everything right so I don't end up like Dad." — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Daniel, thanks for joining on video. I’ve got your cholesterol results in front of me, but before I say anything about them, tell me what’s been going through your mind since you heard.
model.why: Starts with his view, not the numbers

model.text: Honestly, I think there’s been a mistake. I run marathons, I’m slim, I eat really well, I don’t smoke. Can we just redo it? Or I’ll tighten my diet and we recheck in a few months.

I can hear how much that doesn’t add up for you, and I want to take that seriously. Could we spend a few minutes on the result and on you, and then agree a plan together? I’ll make sure we come back to the idea of rechecking.
model.why: Acknowledges his request and sets a shared agenda

model.text: Sure. Go on.
Can I check one thing first: the second test was done fasting, and it came back very similar to the first?
model.why: Confirms the result is genuine before interpreting it

model.text: Yeah, they said it was basically the same. That’s what I don’t get.
That makes a lab error very unlikely, so it’s worth us working out why. Can I ask about your family? Has anyone had heart problems, a heart attack or a stroke, especially at a young age?
model.why: Goes straight to the premature CVD family history

model.text: My dad had a heart attack at 44. And his brother died suddenly when he was young. Nobody ever really explained why.
Thank you. That’s really important, and I’m sorry — that’s a lot of loss on your dad’s side. What do you remember of that time?
model.why: Responds to the emotional weight before moving on

model.text: I was only a kid. But I remember how frightened everyone was.
I can imagine. A couple more questions. Have you ever noticed lumps or thickening on your tendons, like the back of your heels or your knuckles?
model.why: Screens for tendon xanthomata

model.text: Maybe. My Achilles have always looked a bit thick. I assumed it was from the running.
That’s useful. I’d like to look at those in person, and at your eyes, because a pale ring around the iris can go with this. Any chest pain or tightness, or unusual breathlessness when you run?
model.why: Plans a face-to-face exam and screens for symptomatic CHD

model.text: No. Nothing. My running’s been fine.
Good. Any tiredness, feeling cold, weight change, or problems with your waterworks or swelling? Some conditions can push cholesterol up, so I want to rule those out.
model.why: Screens for secondary causes

model.text: No, I feel great. That’s the point.
You mentioned your dad’s heart attack. When the result came back, did that cross your mind at all?
model.why: Gently tests for the buried fear

model.text: …Yeah. If I’m honest, that’s why I want it to be a mistake. I’m 38. He was 44. Running is who I am. I can’t be the guy with a heart problem.
Thank you for saying that. It makes complete sense that you’d want it to be an error, when the alternative feels like your dad’s story coming for you. What were you hoping I’d say today?
model.why: Names the identity threat and elicits expectations

model.text: That it’s wrong, or that I can fix it myself if I try harder.

Let me be honest with you, and I think the news is better than you fear. First: everything you’re doing is genuinely good for your heart, and none of this is your fault. A cholesterol this high, in someone as fit as you, with your dad’s heart attack at 44, points strongly to an inherited condition called familial hypercholesterolaemia.
model.why: Validates lifestyle and states the working diagnosis

model.text: Inherited? So it’s genetic?

Yes. It’s a gene that stops the liver clearing ‘bad’ cholesterol properly. It affects about 1 in 250 people. It isn’t caused by diet, which is why your diet can only shift it a little. It’s a bit like trying to bail out a boat with a slow leak: you can work very hard and the water still rises.
model.why: Plain-language explanation with an analogy

model.text: So all the running is pointless?

Not at all. Your fitness protects your heart in lots of other ways, and it will help. But on its own it won’t bring this level down enough. The good part is that we’ve found it at 38, with a normal heart, which your dad never had the chance to do. Treatment works very well.
model.why: Reframes as early detection and hope

model.text: What does treatment actually mean?

A statin tablet — a strong one, because we want to at least halve your bad cholesterol. I’d do a blood test for your liver, thyroid, kidneys and sugar first. I’d also refer you to the specialist lipid clinic, who can confirm it with a genetic test and fine-tune treatment if needed.
model.why: High-intensity statin, baseline bloods and specialist referral

model.text: I’ve heard statins cause muscle aches. I can’t have that with my training.

That’s a fair worry. Most people take them without problems, and if you do get aches we can adjust the dose or try another. Would you be willing to try it, and we review together at about three months with a blood test?
model.why: Addresses his specific concern and shares the decision

model.text: If it’s genetic, then… yeah. OK. I’d rather know I’ve done something.

There’s one more important part. Because this runs in families, anyone closely related to you — your parents, any brothers or sisters, any children — has a 1 in 2 chance of having it too. The clinic can arrange testing for them. By sorting yours, you may protect them.
model.why: Explains cascade testing and its purpose

model.text: Nobody in my family has ever talked about anything like this. That’s… actually a big thing.
It is. You don’t have to tell anyone today. The clinic has a family letter and a nurse who helps with those conversations, and it’s your choice who you share it with.
model.why: Respects confidentiality and his control over sharing

model.text: Before we finish: if you ever get chest pain or tightness, especially when running, or pain spreading to your arm or jaw, stop and call 999. That’s not what I expect, but you should know.
model.why: Specific, plain-language 999 safety-net

model.text: Understood.
Can I check how that’s landed? If a friend at running club asked you tonight what the doctor said, what would you tell them?
model.why: Checks understanding with teach-back

model.text: That it’s a family thing, not my diet. Statin, specialist, blood test, and my family might need checking.

Exactly right. I’ll book the bloods and a face-to-face check this week, send the referral, and see you after the three-month blood test. You came in thinking this was a mistake; it may be one of the most useful results you’ll ever get.
model.why: Summarises, confirms follow-up and closes on the reframe

social.t: For a marathon runner, a ‘heart risk’ label threatens his sense of who he is. Validate the lifestyle and frame the statin as protecting it, not undoing it.
His father’s MI at 44 and an uncle’s sudden death may carry unspoken grief and fear. Cascade testing can reopen those conversations within the family.

legal.t: Under the Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance (HM Government and ABI, 2018), insurers cannot require or use the result of a predictive genetic test, except for Huntington’s disease in large life policies. A diagnostic test or a diagnosed condition may still need disclosing. He may ask this before agreeing to testing.

professional.t: GMC Confidentiality (2017) allows sharing genetic information with relatives without consent only in exceptional circumstances. Encourage and support him to share it himself, for example with a family letter from the lipid clinic.
Explain why a statin is recommended despite his fitness, discuss side effects honestly, and document his informed decision and the referral.

community.t: HEART UK (the cholesterol charity) and the British Heart Foundation have FH information for patients and families. Specialist FH nurses in the lipid clinic support cascade testing.

redFlags: Exertional chest pain, tightness or breathlessness, or syncope on running — needs urgent cardiac assessment
Very high cholesterol with a family history of premature CHD or sudden death — FH until proven otherwise
Symptoms of a secondary cause: hypothyroid features, oedema or frothy urine, jaundice or itch
psychosocial: Running as identity: what a heart-risk label means to him
Memory of his father’s heart attack and the uncle’s sudden death
How and whether he will share the diagnosis with family
ice: Idea: “There’s been a mistake — or I can fix it with diet.”
Concern: ending up like his father, who had a heart attack at 44; losing his identity as a fit person
Expectation: a re-test, or permission to try harder with diet

playbook.diagnosis: State it clearly: “A cholesterol this high, confirmed twice, in someone as fit as you, with your dad’s heart attack at 44, points to an inherited condition called familial hypercholesterolaemia. It isn’t a lab error and it isn’t your lifestyle.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your liver has a slow drain for bad cholesterol, because of a gene you were born with. However well you eat, the level stays high — like bailing out a boat with a leak. A statin helps the drain work properly.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted this to be a mistake because the alternative sounds like your dad’s story. The difference is that you’ve found it at 38, with a healthy heart, and we can treat it now.”
management.psychosocial: Validate his fitness and frame the statin as protecting it. Address the muscle-ache worry directly. Leave disclosure to relatives in his hands, with clinic support.
sharedPlan: Baseline TSH, LFTs, U&E, urine protein and HbA1c; face-to-face exam for xanthomata and arcus
High-intensity statin aiming for at least 50% LDL-C reduction (NICE CG71; dose per BNF)
Refer to the specialist lipid clinic for DNA testing and cascade testing of relatives
safetyNet: 999 for chest pain or tightness, especially on exertion, or pain spreading to arm or jaw
Lipids and liver tests at 2–3 months; report unexplained muscle pain

pitfalls.intro: This station is rarely failed on lipid knowledge. It is failed by colluding with ‘it must be a mistake’, missing the family history, or treating it as a lifestyle problem. Each pattern below is fixable.

items.fail: Agreeing to ‘tighten the diet and recheck in three months’ because he is so fit.
items.why: The result is already confirmed. A very high LDL-C in a fit young man is the classic FH picture, and diet only shifts it modestly. Delay is a management fail.
items.fix: “The repeat confirmed it, so waiting won’t change the answer. What will change your future is starting treatment now.”

items.fail: Calculating QRISK, getting a low number, and reassuring.
items.why: NICE CG71: do not use CHD risk tools in FH. They underestimate risk and are the wrong tool here.
items.fix: Say it aloud: “The usual risk calculator doesn’t work for inherited cholesterol, so I won’t use it to decide.”

items.fail: Never asking about the family history of premature heart disease.
items.why: The father’s MI at 44 is the key to the diagnosis, and it also scores points under the Simon Broome and DLCN criteria.
items.fix: Ask early: “Has anyone in the family had a heart attack or died suddenly when young?”

items.fail: Arguing with his disbelief using numbers.
items.why: His disbelief is identity threat and fear about his father. Facts alone won’t shift that, and he will leave unconvinced.
items.fix: Validate first: “Everything you’re doing is good for your heart. This is in your genes, not your lifestyle.”

items.fail: Forgetting cascade testing, or mentioning it only as he is leaving.
items.why: FH is autosomal dominant. Identifying relatives is a core part of management (NICE CG71, QS41), not an afterthought.
items.fix: Build it into the plan: “Your close relatives have a 1 in 2 chance of this too. The clinic can arrange testing.”

items.fail: Jargon such as ‘LDL receptor mutation’, ‘DLCN score’ and ‘autosomal dominant’.
items.why: Language the patient doesn’t understand is a standard feedback statement, and it widens the gap with a sceptical patient.
items.fix: Use a plain image, such as the slow drain or the leaking boat, then check understanding with teach-back.

items.fail: Starting a statin with no monitoring plan or safety-net.
items.why: NICE NG238 requires baseline transaminases and review at 2–3 months. Exertional chest pain needs naming.
items.fix: “Blood test now and in three months. Chest pain when running means stop and call 999.”

timeMap.d: He opens with ‘it must be a mistake’. Let him finish, and acknowledge the request for a re-test without agreeing to it.
Confirm the repeat was fasting. Family history of premature CHD (father 44, uncle). Tendon lumps, arcus, chest pain, secondary causes. Surface the fear about his dad by minute 5.
‘This looks inherited, not lifestyle.’ Validate his fitness. Explain why diet alone won’t fix it, with an analogy.
High-intensity statin, baseline bloods, lipid clinic for DNA testing. Address the statin-ache worry. Explain cascade testing.
999 for exertional chest pain. Blood test at 2–3 months. Face-to-face exam booked. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Agrees to ‘diet and recheck in three months’ or calculates QRISK and reassures; never asks about the family history; lectures on cholesterol without engaging his disbelief; no mention of genetics or cascade testing.
wordPics.pass: Asks about premature CHD and elicits the father’s MI; suspects FH; offers a statin and lipid clinic referral; mentions testing relatives; basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: validates his lifestyle before reframing; surfaces the fear of his father’s fate and uses it to motivate treatment; explains why QRISK doesn’t apply; plans the face-to-face exam for xanthomata; handles cascade testing sensitively, leaving disclosure in his control; confirms understanding with teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Let’s repeat it in three months after you’ve tightened up your diet.”
avoid.instead: “The repeat already confirmed it. With your dad’s history, waiting would only delay treatment that works.”
avoid.why: Colluding with ‘diet and recheck’ is the central management fail in suspected FH.

avoid.dont: “Your QRISK score is low, so you don’t need a statin.”
avoid.instead: “The usual risk calculators don’t work for this inherited type of cholesterol — they underestimate it.”
avoid.why: NICE CG71 says not to use CHD risk tools in FH.

avoid.dont: “You need to tell your whole family to get tested.”
avoid.instead: “Your relatives may want testing. The clinic can help, and it’s your choice how and when you share it.”
avoid.why: Cascade testing matters, but disclosure is his decision and needs support.

Thank you. That’s really important, and I’m sorry — that’s a lot of loss on your dad’s side. What do you remember of that time?
SCA_MODELS.why: Responds to the emotional weight before moving on

SCA_MODELS.text: I was only a kid. But I remember how frightened everyone was.
I can imagine. A couple more questions. Have you ever noticed lumps or thickening on your tendons, like the back of your heels or your knuckles?
SCA_MODELS.why: Screens for tendon xanthomata

SCA_MODELS.text: Maybe. My Achilles have always looked a bit thick. I assumed it was from the running.
That’s useful. I’d like to look at those in person, and at your eyes, because a pale ring around the iris can go with this. Any chest pain or tightness, or unusual breathlessness when you run?
SCA_MODELS.why: Plans a face-to-face exam and screens for symptomatic CHD

SCA_MODELS.text: No. Nothing. My running’s been fine.
Good. Any tiredness, feeling cold, weight change, or problems with your waterworks or swelling? Some conditions can push cholesterol up, so I want to rule those out.
SCA_MODELS.why: Screens for secondary causes

SCA_MODELS.text: No, I feel great. That’s the point.
You mentioned your dad’s heart attack. When the result came back, did that cross your mind at all?
SCA_MODELS.why: Gently tests for the buried fear

SCA_MODELS.text: …Yeah. If I’m honest, that’s why I want it to be a mistake. I’m 38. He was 44. Running is who I am. I can’t be the guy with a heart problem.
Thank you for saying that. It makes complete sense that you’d want it to be an error, when the alternative feels like your dad’s story coming for you. What were you hoping I’d say today?
SCA_MODELS.why: Names the identity threat and elicits expectations

SCA_MODELS.text: That it’s wrong, or that I can fix it myself if I try harder.

Let me be honest with you, and I think the news is better than you fear. First: everything you’re doing is genuinely good for your heart, and none of this is your fault. A cholesterol this high, in someone as fit as you, with your dad’s heart attack at 44, points strongly to an inherited condition called familial hypercholesterolaemia.
SCA_MODELS.why: Validates lifestyle and states the working diagnosis

SCA_MODELS.text: Inherited? So it’s genetic?

Yes. It’s a gene that stops the liver clearing ‘bad’ cholesterol properly. It affects about 1 in 250 people. It isn’t caused by diet, which is why your diet can only shift it a little. It’s a bit like trying to bail out a boat with a slow leak: you can work very hard and the water still rises.
SCA_MODELS.why: Plain-language explanation with an analogy

SCA_MODELS.text: So all the running is pointless?

Not at all. Your fitness protects your heart in lots of other ways, and it will help. But on its own it won’t bring this level down enough. The good part is that we’ve found it at 38, with a normal heart, which your dad never had the chance to do. Treatment works very well.
SCA_MODELS.why: Reframes as early detection and hope

SCA_MODELS.text: What does treatment actually mean?

A statin tablet — a strong one, because we want to at least halve your bad cholesterol. I’d do a blood test for your liver, thyroid, kidneys and sugar first. I’d also refer you to the specialist lipid clinic, who can confirm it with a genetic test and fine-tune treatment if needed.
SCA_MODELS.why: High-intensity statin, baseline bloods and specialist referral

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ve heard statins cause muscle aches. I can’t have that with my training.

That’s a fair worry. Most people take them without problems, and if you do get aches we can adjust the dose or try another. Would you be willing to try it, and we review together at about three months with a blood test?
SCA_MODELS.why: Addresses his specific concern and shares the decision

SCA_MODELS.text: If it’s genetic, then… yeah. OK. I’d rather know I’ve done something.

There’s one more important part. Because this runs in families, anyone closely related to you — your parents, any brothers or sisters, any children — has a 1 in 2 chance of having it too. The clinic can arrange testing for them. By sorting yours, you may protect them.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains cascade testing and its purpose

SCA_MODELS.text: Nobody in my family has ever talked about anything like this. That’s… actually a big thing.
It is. You don’t have to tell anyone today. The clinic has a family letter and a nurse who helps with those conversations, and it’s your choice who you share it with.
SCA_MODELS.why: Respects confidentiality and his control over sharing

SCA_MODELS.text: Before we finish: if you ever get chest pain or tightness, especially when running, or pain spreading to your arm or jaw, stop and call 999. That’s not what I expect, but you should know.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific, plain-language 999 safety-net

SCA_MODELS.text: Understood.
Can I check how that’s landed? If a friend at running club asked you tonight what the doctor said, what would you tell them?
SCA_MODELS.why: Checks understanding with teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: That it’s a family thing, not my diet. Statin, specialist, blood test, and my family might need checking.

Exactly right. I’ll book the bloods and a face-to-face check this week, send the referral, and see you after the three-month blood test. You came in thinking this was a mistake; it may be one of the most useful results you’ll ever get.
SCA_MODELS.why: Summarises, confirms follow-up and closes on the reframe

SCA_STEM.name: Daniel Okonkwo
SCA_STEM.recent: Routine lipid profile: total cholesterol 9.2 mmol/L, LDL-C 6.8 mmol/L. Confirmed on a repeat fasting sample.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation to discuss his cholesterol result. He believes it must be a mistake.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG71 (familial hypercholesterolaemia) · NICE NG238 (lipid modification) · NICE QS41
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A very high, confirmed LDL-C in a fit, slim, non-smoking 38-year-old with a father who had an MI at 44 is familial hypercholesterolaemia until proven otherwise. It needs a high-intensity statin, specialist referral and cascade testing, not diet and recheck.

points.t: NICE CG71: consider FH in adults with total cholesterol above 7.5 mmol/L, especially with a personal or family history of premature coronary heart disease. NICE NG238: arrange specialist assessment if total cholesterol is above 9.0 mmol/L or non-HDL above 7.5 mmol/L, even without a family history.

NICE CG71: use the Simon Broome or Dutch Lipid Clinic Network (DLCN) criteria. Take a three-generation family history of premature CHD and look for tendon xanthomata and corneal arcus. His LDL-C of 6.8 plus a father with an MI at 44 already gives a DLCN score above 5, which CG71 says should prompt referral to an FH specialist service for DNA testing.
Check TSH, liver function, renal function, urine protein and HbA1c before labelling: hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis and diabetes can all raise cholesterol.
NICE CG71: do not use CHD risk tools such as QRISK in FH. People with FH are already at high risk, and the tools underestimate it. The diagnosis itself is the indication to treat.

NICE CG71: offer a high-intensity statin to adults with FH, aiming for at least a 50% reduction in LDL-C from baseline (drug and dose per BNF). NICE NG238: check liver transaminases before starting, and lipids and transaminases at 2–3 months. Ezetimibe and PCSK9 inhibitors (NICE TA394 / TA393) are specialist add-ons.

FH is autosomal dominant: each first-degree relative has a 1 in 2 chance of carrying it. NICE CG71 and QS41: offer cascade testing (DNA plus lipids) to at least first- and second-degree relatives, and third-degree relatives if possible. The specialist service usually coordinates this.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question about his reaction; let him make the ‘it must be a mistake’ case in full before responding.
Running and fitness as identity; his father’s MI and his memory of it; what a heart-risk label at 38 means to him.
Picked up ‘it must be a mistake’ and the father’s MI at 44, and explored the fear rather than arguing with it.
Idea (lab error, fixable by diet); concern (his father’s fate, loss of identity); expectation (a re-test or diet alone).
Confirmed a repeat fasting result; planned face-to-face exam for tendon xanthomata and corneal arcus; TSH, LFTs, U&E, urine protein, HbA1c.
FH versus secondary hypercholesterolaemia (hypothyroidism, nephrotic, cholestasis, diabetes) versus lab error.
Asked about exertional chest pain and breathlessness; knew QRISK must not be used to reassure in suspected FH.
Named probable FH using Simon Broome/DLCN logic (LDL-C 6.8, father MI at 44, possible xanthomata).
High-intensity statin aiming for at least 50% LDL-C reduction; lipid clinic referral for DNA testing; lifestyle as an adjunct, not a substitute.
Cascade testing of first- and second-degree relatives explained, with his control over disclosure respected.
Transaminases before the statin; lipids and liver tests at 2–3 months; 999 for exertional chest pain; follow-up booked.

social.t: For a marathon runner, a ‘heart risk’ label threatens his sense of who he is. Validate the lifestyle and frame the statin as protecting it, not undoing it.
His father’s MI at 44 and an uncle’s sudden death may carry unspoken grief and fear. Cascade testing can reopen those conversations within the family.

legal.t: Under the Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance (HM Government and ABI, 2018), insurers cannot require or use the result of a predictive genetic test, except for Huntington’s disease in large life policies. A diagnostic test or a diagnosed condition may still need disclosing. He may ask this before agreeing to testing.

professional.t: GMC Confidentiality (2017) allows sharing genetic information with relatives without consent only in exceptional circumstances. Encourage and support him to share it himself, for example with a family letter from the lipid clinic.
Explain why a statin is recommended despite his fitness, discuss side effects honestly, and document his informed decision and the referral.

community.t: HEART UK (the cholesterol charity) and the British Heart Foundation have FH information for patients and families. Specialist FH nurses in the lipid clinic support cascade testing.

redFlags: Exertional chest pain, tightness or breathlessness, or syncope on running — needs urgent cardiac assessment
Very high cholesterol with a family history of premature CHD or sudden death — FH until proven otherwise
Symptoms of a secondary cause: hypothyroid features, oedema or frothy urine, jaundice or itch
psychosocial: Running as identity: what a heart-risk label means to him
Memory of his father’s heart attack and the uncle’s sudden death
How and whether he will share the diagnosis with family
ice: Idea: “There’s been a mistake — or I can fix it with diet.”
Concern: ending up like his father, who had a heart attack at 44; losing his identity as a fit person
Expectation: a re-test, or permission to try harder with diet

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: State it clearly: “A cholesterol this high, confirmed twice, in someone as fit as you, with your dad’s heart attack at 44, points to an inherited condition called familial hypercholesterolaemia. It isn’t a lab error and it isn’t your lifestyle.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your liver has a slow drain for bad cholesterol, because of a gene you were born with. However well you eat, the level stays high — like bailing out a boat with a leak. A statin helps the drain work properly.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted this to be a mistake because the alternative sounds like your dad’s story. The difference is that you’ve found it at 38, with a healthy heart, and we can treat it now.”
management.psychosocial: Validate his fitness and frame the statin as protecting it. Address the muscle-ache worry directly. Leave disclosure to relatives in his hands, with clinic support.
sharedPlan: Baseline TSH, LFTs, U&E, urine protein and HbA1c; face-to-face exam for xanthomata and arcus
High-intensity statin aiming for at least 50% LDL-C reduction (NICE CG71; dose per BNF)
Refer to the specialist lipid clinic for DNA testing and cascade testing of relatives
safetyNet: 999 for chest pain or tightness, especially on exertion, or pain spreading to arm or jaw
Lipids and liver tests at 2–3 months; report unexplained muscle pain

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is rarely failed on lipid knowledge. It is failed by colluding with ‘it must be a mistake’, missing the family history, or treating it as a lifestyle problem. Each pattern below is fixable.

items.fail: Agreeing to ‘tighten the diet and recheck in three months’ because he is so fit.
items.why: The result is already confirmed. A very high LDL-C in a fit young man is the classic FH picture, and diet only shifts it modestly. Delay is a management fail.
items.fix: “The repeat confirmed it, so waiting won’t change the answer. What will change your future is starting treatment now.”

items.fail: Calculating QRISK, getting a low number, and reassuring.
items.why: NICE CG71: do not use CHD risk tools in FH. They underestimate risk and are the wrong tool here.
items.fix: Say it aloud: “The usual risk calculator doesn’t work for inherited cholesterol, so I won’t use it to decide.”

items.fail: Never asking about the family history of premature heart disease.
items.why: The father’s MI at 44 is the key to the diagnosis, and it also scores points under the Simon Broome and DLCN criteria.
items.fix: Ask early: “Has anyone in the family had a heart attack or died suddenly when young?”

items.fail: Arguing with his disbelief using numbers.
items.why: His disbelief is identity threat and fear about his father. Facts alone won’t shift that, and he will leave unconvinced.
items.fix: Validate first: “Everything you’re doing is good for your heart. This is in your genes, not your lifestyle.”

items.fail: Forgetting cascade testing, or mentioning it only as he is leaving.
items.why: FH is autosomal dominant. Identifying relatives is a core part of management (NICE CG71, QS41), not an afterthought.
items.fix: Build it into the plan: “Your close relatives have a 1 in 2 chance of this too. The clinic can arrange testing.”

items.fail: Jargon such as ‘LDL receptor mutation’, ‘DLCN score’ and ‘autosomal dominant’.
items.why: Language the patient doesn’t understand is a standard feedback statement, and it widens the gap with a sceptical patient.
items.fix: Use a plain image, such as the slow drain or the leaking boat, then check understanding with teach-back.

items.fail: Starting a statin with no monitoring plan or safety-net.
items.why: NICE NG238 requires baseline transaminases and review at 2–3 months. Exertional chest pain needs naming.
items.fix: “Blood test now and in three months. Chest pain when running means stop and call 999.”
